args.user_asks: Keep an eye on this authenticated page and, if a meaningful change appears, tell me what changed, show me the exact evidence, and let me dismiss or reopen it from the pendant.
args.why_useful: This uses the one reach unique to Safari (existing login) while making the result actionable away from the Mac: semantic diffs rather than noisy reloads, provenance the owner can inspect, and a durable wearable alert when the browser is unattended.
args.model_tier: background change detector uses a cheap local/deterministic extractor; realtime tier only turns the selected diff into speech on demand.
args.latency_budget: Polling/diffing within 1–5 minutes of a change; under 3 seconds from pendant request to spoken evidence when Safari is online.
args.cost_estimate: Negligible for polling and hashing; roughly one short realtime turn only when the owner asks for the evidence, with extraction preferably local and no page body sent to the model.
args.security_concerns: The watch is explicitly opt-in per URL/session and should default to no persistence of page text. Store only a short changed-claim capsule, URL, timestamp, and selector provenance under existing browser TTL; surface login/session-expired state rather than attempting credential entry. Dismiss/reopen are reversible; never auto-submit page actions.
missing: A semantic region-watch scheduler that can reuse a live authenticated browser session
A diff evidence capsule with selector/heading provenance and a pendant alert action
An owner-configurable per-origin watch policy, shipped empty

args.user_asks: Read the section I’m looking at in Safari, compare it with the files and notes on my Mac, and tell me whether it contradicts anything I already believe—without saving the page.
args.why_useful: A logged-in page and local documents are two otherwise isolated evidence pools. This gives the owner a private, source-grounded contradiction check from the pendant instead of manually copying sensitive text into chat.
args.model_tier: cheap local extraction and deterministic document search first; use the realtime model only to reconcile the small evidence snippets and speak the conclusion.
args.latency_budget: 3–8 seconds for a focused section and local search; if the page is large, return a staged result within 15 seconds.
args.cost_estimate: Usually one short model turn over truncated snippets; local search and browser extraction dominate, so no whole-page upload or repeated context tax.
args.security_concerns: Read-only browser allow-set (`browser_read_page`/`browser_snapshot`) and read-only local search. Never persist page HTML or snippets; retain only an ephemeral evidence graph for the request, with source URLs and local file paths shown in the spoken result. Empty per-origin policy remains the default until the owner configures it.
missing: A browser selection/focused-region extraction action (not just full-page extraction)
A local read-only evidence-join endpoint that returns citations without storing source text
A privacy-preserving contradiction comparator that expires its working set

args.user_asks: Before I commit this booking or purchase, check the logged-in page against my calendar and preferences, list every mismatch and hidden cost, and leave the final submit untouched.
args.why_useful: It catches date, timezone, duplicate-event, cancellation, and price mistakes at the last safe point—where browser access to the real session and Mac access to the owner's schedule jointly matter. The owner gets a concrete preflight, not a generic page summary.
args.model_tier: deterministic extraction for dates, currency, fees, cancellation terms, and calendar conflicts; a cheaper model summarizes only ambiguous terms; realtime speaks the final checklist.
args.latency_budget: Under 10 seconds for a normal checkout/booking page, with a visible pending state if a terms section needs further extraction.
args.cost_estimate: Low: structured extraction and calendar lookup are local; at most one short model call for ambiguous legal/fee language.
args.security_concerns: Browser actions are read-only through a strict allow-set and stop before submit. Never persist checkout text or payment details; return only mismatch claims and source selectors. The owner can inspect the exact fields and URL before taking the irreversible action.
missing: A structured browser form/checkout extractor for totals, terms, dates, and selected options
A calendar/preference conflict join that understands timezone and duplicate bookings
A pendant-readable preflight card with an explicit 'submit remains untouched' status

args.user_asks: Audit the authenticated services I select for recurring charges or renewals, reconcile them with my local receipts and calendar, and give me one dated cancellation/renewal list—without changing any account.
args.why_useful: The browser can see subscription portals behind logins while the Mac can see local receipts and calendar entries; neither view alone reveals forgotten renewals, duplicate services, or a renewal that conflicts with a planned cancellation.
args.model_tier: background deterministic extraction and entity matching first; a cheap model clusters merchant names and dates; realtime is used only to answer follow-up questions or read the final prioritized list.
args.latency_budget: Run as a user-started batch in 1–3 minutes for 3–5 explicitly selected origins, with progressive results per origin.
args.cost_estimate: Low-to-moderate: browser navigation and local receipt parsing dominate; one compact model call for ambiguous merchant/renewal matching, not a full-page context resend.
args.security_concerns: Start with an empty explicit origin configuration; user selects origins each run. Read-only browser actions, no cancellation clicks, no payment data persistence. Persist only short-lived claims (merchant, amount, renewal date, URL provenance) under existing browser TTL and let the owner delete the resulting report.
missing: A multi-origin browser batch runner that isolates sessions and reports login failures
Receipt/calendar entity resolution with confidence and duplicate suppression
A browser finding schema specialized for recurring-charge evidence and an auditable delete/export report

args.latency_impact: Sub-second for current DOM; up to 2 seconds for an iframe or shadow-root traversal.

transcript.text:
Safari is now live with two tabs; the active tab is YouTube, and the extension is online with no queued commands. I still need:

- The owner’s explicit list of authenticated origins to automate. I will not invent this; the configuration should ship empty.
- A reliable, unambiguous browser read/region command. The currently granted wrappers still resolve ambiguously between `browser_list_tabs`/`browser_list_sessions` and related actions.

This round produced three new capabilities:

1. **Authenticated page change radar** — watch an explicitly selected page, detect semantic changes, send a concise alert to the pendant, and retain only short-lived evidence claims.
2. **Booking/purchase preflight** — before submission, compare dates, timezone, fees, cancellation terms, calendar conflicts, and duplicate bookings; leave the final submit untouched.
3. **Subscription and renewal audit** — reconcile selected authenticated service portals against local receipts and calendar entries, producing a dated renewal/cancellation list without changing accounts.

I also proposed a browser-harness change: a bounded, read-only `browser_extract_region` command for the current selection or CSS region, returning only normalized text plus heading/URL provenance and never persisting page content. It was recorded, though close to an existing selection-capture idea, so I would not repeat it.

args.user_asks: Save my place in this logged-in application, including the fields I have already reviewed and the exact step I reached, then let me resume it later from the pendant or another Mac without submitting anything.
args.why_useful: Today a dropped browser session or interrupted application forces the owner to rediscover where they were, while ordinary page memory cannot safely reconstruct a multi-step authenticated workflow. A resumable checkpoint preserves progress without taking the irreversible action on the owner’s behalf.
args.model_tier: Local extension code captures structured, non-secret form state and step metadata; no model is needed to checkpoint. A cheap model can explain what will be restored; realtime is only for the owner’s resume request.
args.latency_budget: Checkpoint in under 2 seconds; resume preview in under 5 seconds, with a clear stale-session or changed-page result rather than guessing.
args.cost_estimate: Near-zero model cost for capture/restore; one short model turn only if the owner asks for a spoken explanation of the checkpoint.
args.security_concerns: Ship disabled by default until the owner explicitly enables an origin. Never capture passwords, payment numbers, tokens, or full page text. Encrypt checkpoints locally, bind them to origin and page fingerprint, expire them quickly, and restore only into a preview state. Never click submit or final confirmation.

args.user_asks: When a logged-in service changes its terms or privacy policy, show me only the clauses that changed since the last version I approved, explain the practical impact, and keep me from accidentally accepting the new version.
args.why_useful: A normal page reader can summarize today’s document but cannot establish what changed for this particular account. Version-aware, authenticated comparison turns opaque policy updates into a short actionable decision while the browser is still at the acceptance screen.
args.model_tier: Local canonicalization and clause hashing identify changed sections; a cheaper background model summarizes only changed clauses; realtime reads the selected impact summary on demand.
args.latency_budget: Detection during an explicit visit or scheduled check within minutes; comparison and spoken summary within 10 seconds for a normal policy.
args.cost_estimate: Low: hashes and diffs are local; model input is limited to changed clauses rather than whole policies.
args.security_concerns: Owner selects origins explicitly. Store hashes and short clause claims with version/date provenance, not whole policy text. Never click acceptance. Treat inability to verify version identity as an alert, not as approval.
missing: Authenticated policy-version watcher with canonical clause extraction
A durable per-origin approved-version ledger with short-lived source evidence
An acceptance-screen detector that can pause at the decision without mutating the page

args.user_asks: Check the security pages of the accounts I choose, compare recent sign-ins, recovery methods, and active sessions with my known devices, and tell me exactly what looks unfamiliar without changing anything.
args.why_useful: The browser is the only node that can see account-security panels behind existing logins. Combining those panels with the Mac’s actual device state can reveal a compromised session or stale recovery method before it becomes an incident.
args.model_tier: Deterministic extraction and device/session matching first; a background model clusters unfamiliar entries and explains uncertainty; realtime is reserved for an urgent spoken alert or follow-up.
args.latency_budget: A selected-origin audit completes progressively in 30–90 seconds; urgent anomaly alerts reach the pendant as soon as the first high-confidence mismatch is found.
args.cost_estimate: Low-to-moderate: portal navigation is the main cost, with one compact model call for ambiguous device names or locations.
args.security_concerns: Explicit per-origin selection, read-only browser action set, and no password/recovery-secret persistence. Store only an expiring anomaly claim with timestamp, account-origin, and evidence URL. Never revoke sessions, rotate credentials, or edit recovery settings automatically; show the exact proposed remediation separately.
missing: Origin-specific security-page adapters that recognize sign-in, recovery, and active-session records
A local known-device registry tied to Mac hardware identity and owner-approved aliases
High-confidence anomaly scoring with duplicate suppression and pendant escalation

args.user_asks: “While I’m wearing the pendant, check the authenticated pages I already have open, tell me the one thing that needs my attention, and prepare the next action without sending or submitting anything.”
args.why_useful: This is the browser node’s uniquely valuable job: it can see private logged-in pages while the relay hears the owner and the Mac can act. It turns a vague spoken request into a bounded triage: read the live sessions, extract only actionable claims, then prepare (but do not commit) a reminder, draft, or navigation for the owner to inspect.

args.cost_estimate: Usually one cheap extraction/planning call plus a short realtime response; browser and Mac execution dominate latency, not token cost. Avoid sending page bodies to the model—send capped claims and provenance.
args.security_concerns: Authenticated page content leaves Safari only as the minimum extracted claims. Persist findings, not HTML, screenshots, or page text, using the existing 24-hour browser TTL and provenance. Configuration must ship empty and let the owner define per-origin read/extract/redact/never-store and per-category speak/store rules. The browser supplies the authenticated DOM and focused/visible context; the pendant supplies low-friction questions; the relay answers grounded in that exact page rather than guessing from a URL or public search.

Do not persist page contents; retain only a short-lived context ID and any explicitly requested claim under existing browser provenance/TTL rules. The button must not click, type, or submit.

A context lease keyed to tab and page revision, with invalidation on navigation or login change

transcript.text:
Round 219 completed.

I discovered that Safari is now live with **two tabs**, including:

- YouTube: “Max Hodak: Average Is Not Good Enough”
- Safari extension v1.2.0, online, no pending commands

I recorded three new capabilities:

1. **Authenticated open-tab triage** — inspect current logged-in tabs, identify the single actionable item, and prepare (but do not execute) the next Mac action.
2. **Pendant page-grounded Q&A** — press the pendant while viewing a private page and ask spoken questions about the visible/focused section without losing the page context.
3. **Final-form/checkout audit** — extract recipients, amounts, dates, attachments, and changed fields before submission, then leave the page untouched.

What I still need:

- A reliable, non-ambiguous browser read/snapshot command. The Safari session is live, but the granted enqueue wrappers still resolve inconsistently; the existing `/execute` path needs a confirmed browser-read invocation.
- A **revision-bound page-context lease** that expires on navigation or login change, so follow-up questions remain grounded without resending page contents.

- The owner’s eventual per-origin and category policy configuration. It should remain empty until supplied; existing browser retention rules already provide short-lived claims and provenance.
- A first-class orchestration job connecting browser extraction → Mac action preview → pendant summary.

I also notified `mac-planner` of the three proposals and the missing integration seams.

args.user_asks: “Copy the relevant details from this logged-in page into the other logged-in site, translate the fields correctly, and leave the second form ready for review without submitting it.”
args.why_useful: This is a genuinely browser-exclusive capability: the owner’s authenticated data may exist in two separate services that no public API or Mac-only agent can access. It could transfer an address from an account portal into a shipping form, claim details into an insurer form, or an itinerary into a travel site while preserving the owner’s existing sessions. The owner gets the labor-saving part without surrendering control of the irreversible submit.
args.model_tier: A cheaper structured mapper performs field matching, normalization, and validation; realtime is used only for spoken clarification of ambiguous fields. Vision is a fallback for unusual rendered forms.
args.latency_budget: 15–30 seconds for two already-open authenticated tabs. Return a field-by-field transfer report and stop with the destination form staged.
args.cost_estimate: One extraction call, one mapping/validation call, and browser fill actions. Token cost stays bounded by sending only selected source fields and destination labels, never complete page bodies.
args.security_concerns: Cross-origin transfer must be explicit per invocation and limited to fields the owner names or approves. Never copy passwords, MFA codes, payment CVVs, session tokens, or hidden fields. Preserve a reversible field ledger showing source label/value, destination label/value, transformations, and omissions. Do not submit or send. Persist no page text; retain only a short-lived provenance record if the owner asks.
missing: A cross-origin transfer planner that can hold two authenticated browser session handles simultaneously
Schema-aware field matching with normalization, ambiguity reporting, and explicit exclusion of credential/payment fields
A browser fill transaction with per-field undo and a destination-page revision check before each write
A pendant-readable transfer summary and a way to correct one field by voice before staging the rest

args.user_asks: “Compare these two logged-in services and tell me whether they agree—show me exactly where they differ and which page supports each fact.”
args.why_useful: People routinely have conflicting private records: a travel booking versus an airline account, an invoice versus a payment portal, or an appointment portal versus a calendar. Today the system can inspect a page or act on the Mac, but cannot perform a provenance-preserving cross-origin reconciliation. This would return a small evidence-backed discrepancy report instead of a vague summary or an unsafe correction.
args.model_tier: Cheap deterministic extraction and normalization first; a slower background model resolves semantic equivalence and contradictions. Realtime only speaks the conclusion and lets the owner ask about one discrepancy.
args.latency_budget: 20–60 seconds for two or three authenticated pages; stream each source as it arrives and clearly mark unresolved conflicts.
args.cost_estimate: One extraction pass per source and one comparison pass. Keep only compact claims, URLs, timestamps, and field-level evidence; page HTML and screenshots are not sent or stored.
args.security_concerns: Read-only browser actions. The owner chooses the tabs/origins for each comparison; no silent crawling of other sessions. Claims inherit the existing short browser TTL and provenance. Never infer that one source is authoritative without saying so, and never modify either service automatically.
missing: A multi-source comparison job that can bind named source tabs and maintain independent provenance for every claim
A normalization/contradiction engine for dates, amounts, names, statuses, and time zones
A compact evidence capsule that the pendant can identify by source and field without speaking sensitive page text aloud

args.user_asks: “On this private settings page, explain what each available change would affect in my other accounts and devices, then stage only the changes I choose without applying them.”
args.why_useful: Settings pages hide consequential dependencies: changing a forwarding rule, recovery method, privacy switch, subscription tier, or device permission can affect several services. A third idea—resuming interrupted authenticated tasks after login/MFA—was rejected as already present in the backlog, so I did not restate it.

transcript.text:
Recorded three capabilities:

1. **Verified private uploads** — assemble local files for an authenticated upload, show an exact manifest, and require pendant approval before sending.
2. **Resumable authenticated workflows** — checkpoint a web task safely and restore it later after the browser closes, detecting page changes instead of guessing.
3. **Private document/offer comparison** — compare a logged-in web document with a local version and speak the material differences before acceptance.

Each requires new cross-surface coordination among Safari, the Mac, relay, and pendant, rather than merely exposing existing browser controls.

args.user_asks: “What on my logged-in sites actually needs my attention?”

Unlike public search, it reaches sessions only Safari has and produces an actionable answer without reading whole pages aloud.
args.model_tier: Use the realtime tier only for the owner’s short voice request and final one-sentence rendering; use a cheaper background model for per-page extraction and urgency ranking, with deterministic rules first.
args.latency_budget: 15–30 seconds for an on-demand triage; background watches can run on a schedule and alert only on a material change.
args.cost_estimate: Roughly $0.01–$0.08 per run depending on number of pages and extraction calls; browser navigation and deterministic ranking dominate latency, not tokens.
args.security_concerns: Ship with an empty per-origin configuration. The owner later supplies origins and read/extract/redact/never-store rules. Persist only short host-keyed claims under the existing 24-hour/200-character browser-fact limits; never persist HTML, screenshots, or page text. No submit/click mutation in triage.

transcript.text:
Round 228 findings:

- Safari is now online with **2 tabs**; the active tab is YouTube, tab ID `3186198`. There are no pending browser commands. This supersedes the earlier “no tabs” state.

  2. **Browser form drafting with exact payload preview** — fill authenticated forms but never submit until the owner approves the exact recipient, amount, fields, and attachments.
  3. **Active-page conversational capsule** — ask the pendant about the exact Safari tab currently open, with tab identity and a short-lived page-state hash to prevent stale or cross-tab answers.

What I still need:

2. A relay correlation/state hash so a page answer is invalidated if the tab navigates before the response.

args.cost_estimate: Approximately $0.02–$0.15 per meeting hour depending on caption volume and extraction frequency; the dominant cost is rolling caption summarization.
args.security_concerns: The feature must be explicitly started and visibly show recording/indexing state. transcript.text:
Recorded three capabilities:

1. **Private meeting memory** — index authenticated web-meeting captions into ephemeral decisions and answer pendant follow-ups with source timestamps.
2. **Cross-page discrepancy checking** — compare two explicitly selected logged-in pages and speak only material conflicts.
3. **Authenticated dashboard change narration** — interpret private charts visually and report meaningful changes since the last check.

They are not available today because the browser bridge lacks:

- Live caption-delta extraction.
- Two-tab selection and normalized field comparison.
- Structured chart/table extraction with confidence and units.
- Privacy-preserving visual snapshot diffs.
- Session-scoped ephemeral indexes and source-moment references.
- Pendant commands to start/stop these modes and ask follow-ups.

The strongest of these is the **private meeting memory** capability: it would let the owner participate hands-free while retaining decisions without storing a transcript.

args.user_asks: “I’m looking at a page—read the important part and answer my question.”
args.why_useful: This would make the pendant a hands-free lens into authenticated Safari: the owner can ask about a bill, dashboard, or account page without dictating a URL or touching the Mac. The browser supplies the live page, the relay answers briefly, and the pendant speaks it; public pages continue to use cheaper web search.
args.model_tier: Realtime for the short spoken answer; browser extraction and claim compression should be deterministic/local first, escalating to the expensive model only when the question needs interpretation.
args.latency_budget: 4–8 seconds from button/voice request to a one-sentence answer; browser read is usually sub-second and model time dominates.
args.cost_estimate: Roughly one short realtime turn, typically <$0.01–$0.05 depending on model; no page body needs to be resent if the browser emits bounded extracted claims plus a content hash.
args.security_concerns: The active tab may contain secrets. Never send the whole DOM by default: extract the visible/selected region, redact credentials and payment data, and keep the current 24-hour, host-keyed browser-finding retention. The owner already permits browser reads; still stop if the question would cause a mutation.

args.user_asks: “Finish this web form later.” / “Resume the form I started, show me exactly what is filled, and stop before submission.”
args.why_useful: Long authenticated forms are where browser automation loses the owner’s work. A resumable draft would preserve field values and their source, reopen the same session, detect changed or invalid fields, and present a spoken/visual diff before any submit. It is materially different from a one-shot fill: interruption, browser restart, and changed-page recovery are first-class.
args.model_tier: Background/local planner for field mapping and recovery; realtime only for the owner’s short resume/diff conversation. Use deterministic DOM labels and stored provenance before a model.
args.latency_budget: Resume in under 5 seconds; diff generation under 2 seconds for ordinary forms.
args.cost_estimate: Usually <$0.01 per resume when deterministic; model fallback adds a small request only for ambiguous fields. Storage is a few KB of field metadata, not page HTML.
args.security_concerns: Drafts can contain personal and financial data. Encrypt locally, bind them to origin and form fingerprint, expire by default, and never put field values into general memory or speech unless requested. Submission remains an explicit owner action, with a final field/value diff and undoable local draft deletion.

args.cost_estimate: About <$0.05–$0.20 for a small synthesis depending on model and source count; public sources can use web_search/read_web_page, while private page text is bounded claims only.

The result should enumerate source URLs, observation times, and conflicts so stale authenticated pages cannot masquerade as current facts.

I proposed:

transcript.text:
This round established:

- Safari is now online with **4 tabs**, so authenticated browser work is possible.
- The remaining blocker is invocation: the browser wrappers resolve to actions but return `invoked:false`; they do not actually dispatch through `POST /execute`.
- I recorded three new cross-surface workflows:
  1. **Cross-tab reconciliation** — compare claims across two authenticated tabs.
  2. **Session-expiry recovery** — detect logout, reopen the page, and guide the owner without touching passwords or MFA.
  3. **A concrete browser executor** — an unambiguous action enum wired to `POST /execute`, returning tab IDs and normalized results.

I also proposed the highest-value capability again in a refined form: “What’s on the page I’m looking at?” However, the recorder correctly rejected it as already present in the backlog, so I did not count it as new.

What I still need:

1. A callable browser executor using the live spellings: `browser_list_tabs`, `browser_read_page`, `browser_snapshot`, `browser_navigate`, `browser_wait_for`, `browser_click`, and `browser_type`.
2. Stable tab identity in returned results so the pendant can refer to “this page” or “the other tab.”
3. A pendant event wired to a browser-context task.
4. An explicit, initially empty per-origin configuration for authenticated sites; I will not invent the owner’s site list or sensitivity categories.

I’ve notified `mac-planner` that the executor bridge is now the principal blocker.

Never send extracted content to public search or other participants. Do not activate on a page merely because it resembles a meeting.

transcript.text:

This turns the current tab into a private, voice-queryable surface: a single button/utterance can ask about a shipping status, a dashboard value, or a long document. It is more useful than dumping a page because the relay answers only the asked question and the browser evidence can be cited.

Treat a date as untrusted until displayed with its source. Scheduling is a mutation and must be a separate explicit owner command; the browser must never submit forms.

Round 239 produced three new capabilities:

1. **Authenticated Safari Reading List briefing — highest-value item**
   - Voice request: “What are the four newest things in my Safari Reading List, and why might each matter?”
   - Safari extracts only title, URL, and snippet; a background model ranks and summarizes them; the pendant plays four concise sentences.
   - This directly addresses the owner’s repeatedly failed Reading List request.

2. **Privacy-preserving structured browser extraction**
   - Run site-specific, one-shot extraction recipes inside Safari.
   - Return only selected typed fields and provenance—not raw DOM, screenshots, cookies, or full page text.
   - This reduces privacy exposure, latency, and token cost for authenticated tasks.

3. **Authenticated deadline-to-reminder workflow**
   - Extract deadlines from the currently authenticated page.
   - Present normalized candidate reminders, including timezone ambiguity.
   - Create Mac reminders only after explicit spoken approval, with provenance and undo support.

I also confirmed that Safari is now online with **five tabs**, and the Mac bridge is online. The remaining practical gap is not tab availability: it is a reliably callable browser action surface. `browser_run_actions` is the canonical schema, but the currently exposed browser wrappers remain resolver-ambiguous or return descriptions instead of executing. I still need a live callable path for `browser_list_tabs` / `browser_read_page` / `browser_snapshot`, plus a browser-side Reading List extraction action. No owner-specific site list or sensitivity taxonomy is needed yet; those should remain empty, inspectable configuration supplied later by the owner.

Keep it encrypted and local to the Mac where possible, bind it to the Safari tab/origin, expire it after one hour or immediately on request, never include it in general memory, and return 'not in the captured page' rather than infer. The pendant should speak only the selected answer, not the underlying document.

args.user_asks: When a private website shows me something important—an incorrect charge, cancellation, delivery promise, or account status—let me say 'witness this' and get a tamper-evident, time-stamped evidence packet I can later use in a dispute, without storing my credentials or the whole page.

Recorded three new capabilities:

1. **Tamper-evident browser evidence packets** for disputes, preserving selected claims and provenance without credentials or full page storage.
2. **Read-only consequence previews** before cancellations or other account changes, including fees, dates, lost benefits, and reversibility.
3. **Cross-service discrepancy detection** for explicitly selected account fields, with local ephemeral processing and source-level evidence.

Each requires new browser workflows, Mac-local processing, relay provenance/retention support, and concise pendant feedback.

args.user_asks: “What needs my attention in the sites I’m already logged into?”
args.why_useful: This would be the system’s highest-value daily behavior: the relay schedules a browser read of configured authenticated sites, the browser tier extracts only changed/actionable claims, and the pendant delivers a one-sentence alert even if the Mac link later drops. It reaches private pages no other node can reach and avoids making the owner remember to check them.
args.model_tier: Background/scheduled extraction uses a cheap model; realtime is used only if the owner asks a follow-up by voice. A small deterministic change detector should run before any model call.
args.latency_budget: Scheduled checks can take 30–90 seconds and finish asynchronously; an on-demand voice answer should return a short result within 10 seconds, with a durable job receipt if slower.
args.cost_estimate: Roughly $0.01–$0.08 per site check depending on page size and model use; most checks should be zero-model when hashes/selectors show no change. Browser navigation and relay storage dominate operational cost, not tokens.
args.security_concerns: Ship with an empty per-origin configuration; the owner explicitly adds origins and categories. Persist only short claims with URL/evidence, never HTML, page text, or screenshots; retain browser facts for 24 hours and speak only task-matched findings. Filling or sending anything is a separate action and must stop before irreversible submission.
missing: A durable browser watch scheduler that invokes authenticated sessions
An explicit owner-editable per-origin read/extract/redact/never-store configuration UI
A working unambiguous browser action dispatch (the currently granted wrappers still resolve ambiguously)
A relay-to-pendant alert delivery path wired to the accepted offline_alert_inbox behavior

args.user_asks: “What are the four latest items on my Safari Reading List, and read me the first one’s key points?”
args.why_useful: The owner has repeatedly asked this exact question and currently gets failures. Safari’s Reading List is private browser state, not a public web-search problem. A browser extension API could enumerate the list, open only the selected item in the existing authenticated session, extract a short cited summary, and send it to the pendant for playback.
args.model_tier: Use deterministic Safari Reading List enumeration and a cheap summarizer; invoke the realtime model only for an interactive follow-up such as “skip this and read the next.”
args.latency_budget: List enumeration under 2 seconds; selected-page extraction and summary under 15 seconds, with a queued audio result if navigation or login refresh is slow.
args.cost_estimate: About $0.005–$0.03 per selected article; list enumeration itself is negligible. Token usage is bounded by extracting only the selected article’s relevant text.
args.security_concerns: Reading List titles/URLs and article text are private. Keep them on-device where possible, do not persist article bodies, and retain only a short 24-hour claim with URL provenance if the owner asks follow-up questions. Never mark items read, delete entries, or share/send anything without an explicit separate command.
missing: Safari extension permission/API for Reading List enumeration (the current page-action bridge cannot see browser chrome state)
A stable read-only endpoint exposing ordered Reading List metadata to the browser tier
A result handoff that can stage summarized audio for the pendant

args.user_asks: “Fill out this logged-in web form from my notes, check every field and tell me exactly what would be submitted—do not submit it.”
args.why_useful: This combines the browser’s private session with the Mac notes/files tier and the pendant’s concise spoken confirmation. The system can do the tedious field mapping and validation, expose a complete preflight diff, and leave the owner with a ready form rather than risking a blind submission. It is useful for applications, support forms, and reimbursement pages where the browser session is the only authenticated route.
args.model_tier: Use a cheap structured extraction model for note-to-field mapping and deterministic DOM validation; realtime is reserved for answering a field-level spoken question. No model should invent a missing value.
args.latency_budget: Initial field inventory in 5–10 seconds; fill and validation in under 30 seconds. The dashboard and spoken result should show unresolved fields rather than waiting indefinitely.
args.cost_estimate: About $0.02–$0.10 per form depending on fields and note context. Browser round trips and screenshot/DOM extraction dominate; keep screenshots ephemeral and avoid sending them to a cloud model when DOM labels suffice.
args.security_concerns: Read and reversible field edits are allowed by the owner, but the workflow must have a hard pre-submit boundary: no click on submit, send, purchase, delete, or equivalent. Show field, value, source note, and validation status; redact secrets from receipts and retain only provenance plus a user-approved draft. The owner’s existing destructive-action confirmation policy remains the final boundary.
missing: A form-schema extractor that reports submit controls and equivalent high-impact buttons before filling
A draft/undo journal for browser field mutations, including the originating note and exact old value
A spoken and dashboard preflight renderer that can enumerate long forms without leaking sensitive values

args.user_asks: “Compare the options in these logged-in tabs, tell me which is best under my constraints, and leave the chosen option open without buying or booking.”
args.why_useful: The browser can see private prices, availability, account-specific offers, and policy text that public search cannot. It can normalize several tabs into a spoken comparison, preserve the exact evidence links, and position Safari on the recommended option while stopping before the irreversible purchase or booking step.
args.model_tier: Use deterministic extraction for price, dates, fees, and cancellation terms; a cheap reasoning model ranks options against the owner’s stated constraints. Realtime is only for a follow-up such as changing the budget.
args.latency_budget: Collect 3–8 tabs in 20–45 seconds; speak a compact recommendation as soon as the comparison is complete, with a longer evidence table available in the dashboard.
args.cost_estimate: About $0.03–$0.15 per comparison depending on tabs and text length. DOM extraction and navigation are the main latency costs; deduplicate repeated headers before model input.
args.security_concerns: Do not expose account identifiers or persist page bodies. Keep only normalized claims and source URLs with short browser TTL. Never click purchase, reserve, accept terms, or equivalent; show the exact target and total before any future action. The owner’s maximum-access policy permits browsing, while destructive confirmation remains applicable to committing the transaction.
missing: A multi-tab capture coordinator with stable tab IDs and per-tab provenance
A constraint-aware comparison schema for totals, fees, dates, and cancellation terms
A reliable browser command resolver; current granted wrappers ambiguously match browser_list_tabs/browser_list_sessions and cannot execute
A dashboard view for evidence and an explicit commit handoff

Remove near-synonym candidates such as browser_list_sessions from the resolver’s browser action namespace, and return structured command results including tabId, URL, title, and error class.

args.cost_impact: Negligible API cost; a few engineering hours and no hardware cost.

POST /execute browser action dispatch
An explicit resolver inventory that excludes ambiguous aliases

transcript.text:
Three new capabilities were recorded:

1. **Safari Reading List briefing** — enumerate the owner’s private Reading List, summarize a selected item, and stage it for pendant playback without deleting or marking anything read.
2. **Authenticated form preflight** — populate a logged-in form from Mac notes, validate every field, show exactly what would be submitted, and stop before submission.
3. **Private-tab comparison** — compare options across authenticated tabs, cite the evidence, leave the recommendation open, and never purchase or book.

I also recorded a browser-harness change: make the action resolver use one exact set of names (`browser_list_tabs`, `browser_read_page`, `browser_press_key`, etc.). Safari is online with two tabs, but the currently granted wrappers still fail before execution because `browser_list_tabs` is ambiguously matched with `browser_list_sessions`.

What I still need:

- A working, unambiguous browser command dispatch path.
- Safari Reading List enumeration through an extension or Mac bridge API; page actions alone cannot see browser chrome state.
- A form schema/preflight journal that identifies submit-equivalent controls and supports undo.
- A multi-tab capture/comparison coordinator with stable tab IDs and provenance.
- The owner’s explicit per-origin browser configuration when he is ready; it should remain empty rather than assuming sites or sensitivity categories.

args.user_asks: “Forget everything the browser has learned about me since I left home, everywhere—not just the current page—and tell me when it is gone.”
args.why_useful: A browser agent can accumulate private claims across authenticated sites, relay jobs, provenance, and pending audio. The owner needs a single spoken emergency wipe that is stronger than deleting one finding: revoke queued browser work, erase browser-derived memory and evidence capsules, clear staged summaries, and confirm each surface’s completion. A physical pendant action provides a trustworthy fallback when the Mac is unattended.
args.model_tier: Deterministic deletion and receipt generation only; no model call is needed. Realtime is used solely to answer a follow-up about what categories were removed.
args.latency_budget: Acknowledge immediately, complete within 10 seconds for local stores and within 60 seconds for queued relay/browser work. If a surface is offline, show it as pending rather than claiming success.
args.cost_estimate: Negligible token cost; dominated by storage deletion and delivery receipts.
args.security_concerns: This is intentionally destructive and must require an explicit spoken confirmation or a dedicated long press. It must distinguish browser-derived facts from owner-authored notes, preserve only an audit tombstone saying a wipe occurred, and avoid logging the deleted values in command receipts. A pending offline surface must remain visibly unresolved.
missing: One coordinated browser-privacy wipe operation spanning memory, provenance, spool, jobs, and staged audio
A pendant emergency-wipe gesture and authenticated status response
Per-surface deletion receipts with offline retry and no sensitive payloads
Dashboard controls showing exactly what was and was not erased

args.user_asks: “Why did you tell me that? Show me the exact private page evidence, what has changed since you read it, and whether I should still trust the answer.”
args.why_useful: Private web facts expire quickly and can be wrong after a page changes. This capability would let the owner audit a spoken answer without rereading an entire site: revisit the source in the existing authenticated session, compare the captured claim with the current DOM, report changed fields, and downgrade or retract the answer when necessary.
args.model_tier: Use deterministic provenance lookup and field diffs first; a cheap model explains the difference. Realtime handles only the owner’s conversational “what changed?” follow-up.
args.latency_budget: Return provenance immediately from stored receipts; refresh and compare the source within 15 seconds, or clearly label it unverified if navigation fails.
args.cost_estimate: About $0.01–$0.05 per refresh, usually less when the claim has expired or the page is unchanged. Store compact field-level diffs rather than page copies.
args.security_concerns: Never speak or persist unrelated page content while auditing. Restrict the refresh to the original origin and tab/session, redact account identifiers, and keep only the claim, URL, timestamp, and changed-field summary under the existing short browser TTL.
missing: A claim-level evidence capsule with selector or semantic-anchor information sufficient to locate the same field again
A current-versus-captured browser diff engine that can distinguish changed content from layout churn
A pendant-friendly citation token so the owner can ask about a spoken claim without repeating sensitive text

args.user_asks: “If the site changes or logs me out while you are working, recover safely, tell me exactly where you stopped, and let me resume from the same point later.”
args.why_useful: Long authenticated browser tasks currently fail opaquely when a session expires, a tab closes, or a page changes shape. A resumable browser transaction would checkpoint intent, tab identity, extracted non-sensitive state, and the last completed reversible step, then notify the pendant and offer a precise resume rather than restarting or guessing.
args.model_tier: Use deterministic checkpoints, selectors, and session-state checks; use a cheap model only to re-identify a changed page region. Realtime is reserved for resolving an ambiguous resume choice with the owner.
args.latency_budget: Detect failure on each browser result; announce a failure within 2 seconds. Resume should take under 15 seconds when the session remains valid, and otherwise stop at the login wall.
args.cost_estimate: Roughly $0.005–$0.04 per resumed task; most checkpoints are metadata-only. Costs rise only when a changed page requires semantic re-identification.
args.security_concerns: Never checkpoint passwords, tokens, full page text, or screenshots. Bind checkpoints to origin, tab/session, and task hash; invalidate them after the existing browser-fact TTL or on logout. Resumption must not silently cross origins or pass a submit/purchase boundary.
missing: A durable browser transaction/checkpoint format with reversible-step receipts
Session-expiry and tab-loss detection in the extension bridge
A resume protocol that can revalidate origin and page state before continuing
Pendant and dashboard controls for pause, discard, and resume

transcript.text:
Recorded three capabilities:

- **Emergency browser-data wipe:** one confirmed command removes browser-derived memory, provenance, queued work, and staged audio across the browser, relay, Mac, and pendant, with honest per-surface receipts.
- **Private-answer audit:** ask why a spoken answer was given; the system revisits the authenticated source, compares the original claim with current content, and retracts or downgrades stale information.
- **Resumable authenticated browser tasks:** checkpoint reversible progress, detect logout/tab loss/page changes, announce the exact stopping point on the pendant, and resume only after revalidating origin and page state.

Each requires new coordination primitives rather than merely exposing today’s existing browser actions.

args.user_asks: “I’m looking at a logged-in web page—tell me what matters, and answer follow-up questions about it through the pendant.”
args.why_useful: This is the highest-value thing the system can do that no Mac-only agent can: the browser extension sees the authenticated page, while the pendant gives the owner hands-free access. It turns a private dashboard, invoice, reservation, or document into a spoken, queryable interface without asking the owner to copy text or expose credentials.
args.model_tier: Use the cheaper background model for page extraction and claim formation; use realtime only for the owner's short spoken question and answer. Escalate to the expensive model only when the page is ambiguous or the owner asks for synthesis across sections.
args.latency_budget: Initial page read 3–8 seconds; follow-up answers under 2 seconds when based on the extracted claim capsule. Browser navigation/read is allowed, but never submit forms or send messages as part of this capability.
args.cost_estimate: Typically one extraction call plus short realtime turns, roughly $0.01–$0.08 per page depending on length; the browser round trip, not tokens, dominates latency.
args.security_concerns: Credentials remain in Safari. Send only the visible page text/structured claims needed for the question to the model; do not retain HTML, screenshots, or full page text. Use the existing 24-hour, 200-character-per-claim browser memory policy and task-match projection. The empty per-origin policy must remain configurable rather than inventing an allowlist.
missing: A reliable browser_read_page/current-tab action (the existing POST /execute browser actions work, but the granted wrapper is ambiguous)
A page-context session ID linking the active Safari tab, extracted claims, and the next pendant utterance
A compact spoken disambiguation protocol when multiple page regions match the question

args.user_asks: “Pull the due date and amount from this logged-in page and put a reminder on my Mac, with a link back to the exact page.”
args.why_useful: It closes the loop between a private browser page and an action the owner can actually use. Today the browser can read but cannot safely hand a grounded fact into Mac reminders as one coherent job. The owner gets a reminder created from evidence rather than manually transcribing a bill, renewal, appointment, or application deadline.
args.model_tier: Background model extracts a small typed fact set (amount, date, title, URL, confidence); realtime only confirms the spoken request and reports completion. Use a cheaper deterministic date/amount parser before invoking a model.
args.latency_budget: Read and extraction in 5–10 seconds; reminder creation in another 1–3 seconds. Stop if date or amount is ambiguous and speak the competing candidates.
args.cost_estimate: About $0.005–$0.04 per invocation; browser extraction and Mac action are the dominant work, not generation.
args.security_concerns: Only pass extracted fields and provenance, not the page body. The reminder text must not include secrets or account numbers. Keep the source URL and claim evidence capsule under the existing short-lived browser-finding rules; reminder creation is reversible and must produce a job receipt/undo handle.
missing: A typed browser-finding-to-Mac-action handoff carrying claim, confidence, URL, and evidence capsule
A date/amount ambiguity response that returns choices to the pendant instead of guessing
A reminder receipt that embeds provenance and can undo both the reminder and the browser finding

args.user_asks: “Fill this logged-in web form from the details in my Mac, then read me every field and leave it ready for me to submit.”
args.why_useful: Form entry is where browser access saves real time, yet the dangerous part is silent transcription into a private site. This capability combines Safari's session with local facts, performs the reversible fill, and gives the owner a precise spoken audit while deliberately stopping before submit. It is useful for applications, checkout drafts, insurance forms, and scheduling pages.
args.model_tier: Use a cheaper extraction/field-matching model for labels and values; realtime only narrates the compact field diff. Use the expensive tier only for conflicting candidate values or unfamiliar form structure.
args.latency_budget: Inspect and map fields in 5–12 seconds; fill in under 5 seconds; spoken audit starts immediately after the browser result. Never wait on a model while a high-impact submit action is queued.
args.cost_estimate: Roughly $0.01–$0.06 per form, dominated by page snapshots and field mapping; no model call is needed for deterministic local fields.
args.security_concerns: Values come from local Mac sources and may include sensitive identity data. Keep them in memory for the job, redact them from ordinary logs, and store only field names, hashes, origin, and undo metadata. The browser action allow-set should be fill-only; submit, send, purchase, and upload must be impossible in this mode. Provide a complete before/after field diff on the pendant and Mac.
missing: A browser fill transaction with an explicit fill-only action set and rollback of all modified fields
A local-source selector that lets the owner choose which Mac facts may populate each field without inventing site-specific rules
A compact spoken field-diff renderer and a browser job receipt containing an undo token

args.user_asks: “Compare the prices and terms across the private sites I already have open, tell me which is best, and prepare the cheapest option without buying anything.”
args.why_useful: Public search cannot see member pricing, account-specific offers, or the owner's existing subscriptions. The browser can inspect multiple authenticated origins; the Mac can normalize currencies and terms; the pendant can deliver a short recommendation while preserving control. This is a genuinely multi-node advantage, especially for renewals, travel, insurance, and recurring services.
args.model_tier: Use a background model for parallel extraction and normalization, with deterministic currency/date arithmetic. Use realtime only for the recommendation and a follow-up such as “why?”; use the expensive tier for ambiguous terms, not routine page reading.
args.latency_budget: Inspect 2–5 open tabs in 10–20 seconds and produce a ranked comparison in under 30 seconds. Preparation may fill a reversible cart or quote form, but purchase, cancellation, or submission is outside the action set.
args.cost_estimate: Approximately $0.03–$0.20 per comparison, mostly multiple browser snapshots and the cross-page synthesis; subsequent follow-ups reuse short-lived claims.
args.security_concerns: Do not persist page bodies, payment details, or account identifiers. Keep per-origin provenance and 24-hour claim TTL. An explicit empty origin configuration must govern which origins can be compared; when absent, restrict the first run to tabs the owner explicitly names. Never use a hidden logged-in tab as an unspoken source. The result should explain assumptions and show source URLs.
missing: A multi-tab browser job that binds an explicit user-selected tab set and refuses unselected origins
A schema for comparable offer claims (total cost, recurring cost, term, exclusions, cancellation, expiry) with confidence and source ranges
A reversible “prepare but do not buy” browser action mode that can fill quote/cart state and roll it back

args.change: Add a live, privacy-minimal browser context channel: Safari heartbeat reports the owner-selected tab's title, origin, tab ID, and whether text is selected, plus an explicit “owner invoked context” event from the pendant. It must report metadata only until that invocation, then issue one scoped browser_read_page/snapshot job and expire the context after the answer.
args.why_useful_to_owner: The owner can say “this” while looking at a private page and get help without naming a URL, copying text, or accidentally having the system inspect unrelated tabs. It makes the pendant feel present in the browser rather than forcing a separate navigation command.
args.effort: Medium: extension heartbeat/context payload, relay correlation to the pendant utterance, and a one-shot scoped read job with expiry.
args.risk: A stale active-tab ID could read the wrong page; show the origin/title in the spoken or Mac confirmation and reject a context older than a few seconds. If the extension disconnects, fall back to asking the owner to name the page.
args.cost_impact: Negligible API cost for metadata; one normal browser read per explicit invocation. No new hardware cost.
args.latency_impact: Removes a navigation/list-tabs round trip; answer should be 1–3 seconds faster.
args.security_impact: Improves privacy by making content reads explicit and one-shot, but tab title/origin metadata still leaves the device. Never persist metadata beyond the short session and honor the existing empty per-origin configuration.
depends_on: A functioning extension heartbeat payload beyond tabCount/tabUrl
POST /pipeline/events carrying the pendant invocation ID
POST /execute browser_read_page/browser_snapshot scoped to the reported tab ID
Existing browser provenance and short-lived browser-memory policy

args.user_asks: “Use the reservation page I’m viewing to prepare me for leaving: put the appointment on my calendar, check the travel time on my iPhone, and tell me when I need to go.”
args.why_useful: This joins three otherwise disconnected realities: the authenticated reservation contains the authoritative time and address, the Mac can create the local event, and iPhone control can estimate the real departure time. The pendant then gives one concise reminder instead of making the owner transcribe a booking and separately plan travel.
args.model_tier: Background model extracts the reservation fields and resolves timezone/address; deterministic calendar and travel calculations do the rest. Realtime is only for the spoken confirmation or an ambiguity question.
args.latency_budget: Extract in 5–10 seconds, create the calendar event in 1–3 seconds, and obtain a travel estimate in under 15 seconds. If location permission or route data is unavailable, create the event but explicitly omit the departure estimate.
args.cost_estimate: About $0.01–$0.08 per invocation; browser extraction and route lookup dominate. Repeated reminders reuse the event metadata rather than re-reading the page.
args.security_concerns: Reservation codes, addresses, and travel history are sensitive: pass only the event fields to the Mac/iPhone tiers, redact confirmation numbers from spoken output, and store source provenance under the browser 24-hour TTL. Require the owner to name the destination tab or explicitly invoke the page context; never scrape all open tabs. Calendar creation should return an undoable receipt.
missing: A browser-to-calendar typed reservation schema with timezone and confidence
An iOS travel-time action exposed through the Mac iPhone-Mirroring facet
A single job coordinator that waits for browser, calendar, and route results and handles partial completion cleanly

transcript.text:
Round 245 findings:

- Safari is now online with **2 tabs**. The active page is a YouTube video, and a direct `POST /execute` with `browser_snapshot` succeeded, returning 25 interactive elements.
- The generic browser wrappers remain unreliable: `browser_read_or_navigate(browser_list_tabs)` is still ambiguous, although direct `/execute` browser actions work.
- I recorded three new directions:
  1. **Reservation page → calendar + iPhone travel plan + pendant departure alert**.
  2. **Live minimal browser context channel**, so “this page” from the pendant reads only the explicitly invoked tab.
  3. **Authenticated page → grounded Mac reminder**, extracting dates/amounts with provenance and undo support.
- Two proposals collided with existing backlog ideas and were intentionally not repeated: generic authenticated-page Q&A and private-site price comparison. A form-fill audit was recorded but identified as close to existing work.

What I still need is not another browser command wrapper name. The practical missing pieces are:

1. A reliable, unambiguous `browser_read_page`/active-tab action path through the granted tool or a documented direct `/execute` schema.
2. A typed handoff joining browser claims to Mac calendar/reminder actions, including confidence, URL provenance, and undo.
3. An iPhone travel-time action exposed through the Mac/iPhone-mirroring facet.
4. The owner’s eventual per-origin configuration; it should remain empty until they specify which authenticated sites may be read or retained.

Biggest unknown: whether the currently live Safari tabs are owner-intended work or merely incidental. I would not inspect beyond metadata/page structure without an explicit page-context invocation.

args.user_asks: “Build me a support-case packet from this private order page and the relevant emails/files on my Mac, then draft the exact message and leave it unsent.”
args.why_useful: When something goes wrong with a purchase, reservation, or account, the evidence is split between an authenticated webpage and local mail/files. Today no single node can assemble a grounded chronology, identify the missing proof, and prepare a useful support request. The owner gets a complete, reviewable packet instead of hunting through tabs and attachments.
args.model_tier: Use a background model to extract a structured chronology and deduplicate evidence; use realtime only to answer the owner's questions and read the short draft aloud. Use the expensive tier only for contradictory dates or policy language.
args.latency_budget: Collect and index the selected page plus named local sources in 15–30 seconds; produce a draft in under 45 seconds. Never send, upload, or submit anything automatically.
args.cost_estimate: Approximately $0.05–$0.30 per packet, dominated by document extraction and attachment OCR; later edits should reuse the local evidence index.
args.security_concerns: This may contain names, addresses, order IDs, and correspondence. The owner must explicitly select the browser tab and local folder/mail thread; do not search the whole mailbox or all tabs. Store a manifest of source hashes, URLs, and filenames rather than copied page bodies; redact payment credentials and unrelated recipients. The generated message must clearly show recipients, attachments, and claims before any future send action.
missing: A cross-surface evidence collector that accepts an explicit Safari tab plus explicit Mac files/mail threads
A provenance-preserving chronology and contradiction detector that can cite each claim back to its source
A draft-message and attachment staging object with reversible cleanup, separate from any send/upload action
A pendant-friendly review protocol that summarizes the packet and lets the owner request a specific citation or correction

args.user_asks: “Audit the privacy and security settings in this logged-in account, explain what changed since last time, and prepare recommendations without changing anything.”
args.why_useful: Account settings are private, fragmented, and often impossible to evaluate from public documentation. The browser can inspect the real effective settings, while the Mac can compare a prior claim set and the pendant can explain the few consequential changes. This gives the owner an actionable security review without granting the system permission to alter protections.
args.model_tier: Use a background model for structured setting extraction and diffing; realtime handles only the spoken summary and owner questions. Use the expensive model for ambiguous policy wording or conflicting controls.
args.latency_budget: Scan a named settings area in 10–20 seconds and report material changes in under 30 seconds. Do not crawl beyond the explicitly selected account area.
args.cost_estimate: About $0.03–$0.15 per audit, driven by several page reads and policy-text comparison; incremental audits are cheap if only changed claims are retained.
args.security_concerns: Security settings themselves are sensitive. Persist only normalized setting names, values, host, timestamp, and provenance—not screenshots, tokens, recovery codes, or page bodies. Never click save, enable, disable, revoke, or rotate. The owner must explicitly invoke the audit on the current account and receive a clear scope statement.
missing: A typed security-setting schema with impact labels and effective-vs-inherited state
A host-scoped historical diff store for short normalized claims, with expiration and deletion
A browser read-only scope that can traverse settings navigation but cannot mutate controls
A spoken prioritization rubric that distinguishes urgent exposure from harmless presentation changes

args.user_asks: “For this private account, tell me what data it holds, what I would lose by closing it, and prepare an export or closure request without submitting it.”
args.why_useful: Public help pages cannot reveal the account's actual stored profile, subscriptions, credits, active sessions, or deletion consequences. The browser extension can inspect the authenticated account while the Mac organizes a private checklist and the pendant gives a plain-language decision brief. It helps the owner leave services deliberately instead of discovering irreversible losses afterward.
args.model_tier: Background model extracts account-specific assets, dependencies, and export options; deterministic checklists handle counts and dates. Realtime is reserved for the owner's decision questions, not the full page scrape.
args.latency_budget: Produce an inventory in 20–40 seconds across the explicitly selected account pages. Preparing a draft export/deletion request may take another 5 seconds, but no destructive control is ever activated.
args.cost_estimate: Roughly $0.05–$0.25 per account, depending on the number of settings and export pages; retain only compact claims so follow-up questions are inexpensive.
args.security_concerns: Never download or persist the account's full data export by default. Do not expose recovery codes, payment details, private messages, or session tokens in speech. Require explicit owner selection of the account and a visible list of planned fields/actions. Export, close, revoke, and submit controls must remain outside the read-and-prepare action set.
missing: An account-asset inventory schema covering subscriptions, credits, stored content, integrations, sessions, and deletion dependencies
A browser workflow that discovers export/closure prerequisites without activating them
A local decision brief with citations and a reversible draft request object
A retention/deletion control allowing the owner to purge the extracted account inventory immediately

transcript.text:
Recorded three capabilities:

- Private support-case evidence packets from authenticated pages plus local mail/files.
- Read-only security and privacy setting audits with historical diffs.
- Account-data inventory and export/closure preflight without submission.

Each requires explicit page/source scope, provenance-aware extraction, and a strict separation between preparation and irreversible actions.

args.user_asks: “What am I looking at right now, and what do I need to know?” — read the active authenticated Safari tab, answer a question about it, and speak only the concise answer through my pendant.
args.why_useful: This is the browser node's unique reach: it can see pages behind the owner's existing logins while the relay can converse and the pendant can deliver an answer hands-free. It turns the current tab into an on-demand private assistant without requiring the owner to copy/paste or expose page text to durable memory. The answer should carry the page title/URL and a live evidence capsule, and expire with the turn.
args.model_tier: Use gpt-5.6-luna on the Mac/browser tier for extraction and gpt-realtime-2.1 only for the short conversational response; do not send raw page text into long-lived context.
args.latency_budget: 2–5 seconds for read plus synthesis; if the page is still loading, say so rather than silently answering from a stale tab.
args.cost_estimate: About one browser action and a short low-token realtime response; typically far cheaper than a full long-context turn. Dominant cost is page text sent once for extraction.
args.security_concerns: Never persist HTML, screenshots, or page text. Keep claims under the existing browser TTL/length limits, join them only to this task, and return the exact origin/title so the owner can catch a wrong-tab answer. Require an explicit per-origin configuration later; ship empty rather than guessing which logged-in sites are acceptable.
missing: A first-class active-tab read that guarantees the requested tab identity (the live harness currently returned YouTube content when asked for the DoorDash tab)
A relay intent that binds a spoken question to a single browser evidence capsule and suppresses durable storage

args.change: Make browser actions tab-addressed and fail closed on identity mismatch. Before every browser_read_page/click/type/snapshot, resolve the requested tabId and return an error if the extension replies with a different tabId, URL, or title; never substitute the active tab. Include requestedTab and observedTab in the receipt, and require a fresh list_tabs after navigation before allowing a follow-up action.
args.why_useful_to_owner: Today a read requested for the DoorDash tab returned the active YouTube page instead, with a successful receipt. A spoken answer could therefore confidently describe the wrong logged-in page. This change makes browser assistance trustworthy: wrong-tab or closed-tab conditions become an explicit, recoverable message instead of a plausible lie.
args.effort: Medium: thread tabId through browserBridge/browserPage and add a result validator plus regression tests for two tabs, navigation, and extension races.
args.risk: Some existing flows that implicitly use the active tab will start returning a clear mismatch error; recover by refreshing tab inventory and retrying against the observed tab only. No page mutation is introduced.
args.cost_impact: Negligible runtime/API cost; modest engineering/test cost.
args.latency_impact: Adds one local tab-resolution/validation step, generally under 100 ms; a recovery retry may add one browser round trip.
args.security_impact: Positive: prevents cross-tab leakage between authenticated origins and makes provenance honest. It does not create an origin policy, so the owner's explicit per-origin configuration remains separate.
depends_on: Existing POST /execute browser_* action path and browser result provenance
Existing GET /browser/inspect and tabId-bearing browser receipts

args.user_asks: “Check this booking/order against my calendar and tell me if anything conflicts.”
args.why_useful: The browser can read the authenticated confirmation the owner is already viewing, while the Mac can read Calendar and the relay can reconcile dates, times, locations, and names. Today each node sees only its own surface; this catches double-bookings, impossible travel, duplicate charges, or a wrong date at the moment the owner is looking at the confirmation. The pendant delivers the result without requiring the owner to keep the page open or copy details.
args.model_tier: Use gpt-5.6-luna locally for structured extraction and deterministic date/time normalization, with a small gpt-5.6-luna judgement pass for conflicts; use realtime only to state the result. Do not use the expensive realtime tier to parse a whole page.
args.latency_budget: 4–8 seconds for one page plus a calendar window; return ‘could not verify’ for missing timezone/location rather than guessing.
args.cost_estimate: One browser read and one local Calendar read plus a compact structured comparison; low token cost because only normalized fields cross surfaces.
args.security_concerns: Never persist confirmation HTML or full calendar entries. Keep only a short, task-scoped conflict claim with URL/title provenance and existing 24-hour browser TTL. Do not assume which origins/categories are acceptable: an empty per-origin policy must be configurable by the owner.
missing: A structured browser extractor that emits typed fields (date, timezone, location, amount, confirmation status) with evidence spans
A cross-surface join that can request a bounded Calendar interval and reconcile timezones/locations
A pendant response template for conflicts that does not read sensitive booking details aloud unless requested

args.user_asks: “Is this page safe to use, or does anything look suspicious?”
args.why_useful: A worn-device owner often opens a link in an already-authenticated browser before noticing a look-alike domain, unexpected payment destination, or request for credentials. The browser supplies the exact origin, redirect chain, visible form fields, and page evidence; the Mac checks the connection/domain metadata; the relay compares the signals and speaks a short warning through the pendant. This is a capability no pendant-only or Mac-only node can provide because the browser session is the only place where the real page and login state coexist.
args.model_tier: Use deterministic origin/redirect/form heuristics first and a cheap background gpt-5.6-luna judgement pass for ambiguous page language. Reserve gpt-realtime-2.1 for the owner's follow-up conversation, not page scanning.
args.latency_budget: Under 3 seconds for URL/origin checks and under 8 seconds for an ambiguous content verdict; an immediate ‘do not enter credentials yet’ warning should precede deeper analysis.
args.cost_estimate: Low: one page snapshot/read and local metadata checks, with a small extracted-text prompt. Dominant cost is only ambiguous pages sent for model review.
args.security_concerns: Treat this as advisory, never as proof of legitimacy. Do not transmit secrets or form values; redact credential/payment fields before analysis and never persist page text/screenshots. The owner must see the exact origin and redirect chain, and any click/type remains separately requested. Use the empty per-origin configuration rather than inventing an allowlist.
missing: A local certificate/redirect/origin inspection action paired with the browser tab
A redaction-aware page classifier for login/payment/credential requests
A pendant warning event with severity and URL spoken only on request

args.subject: Live browser correctness bug found

I recorded a browser-harness change to fail closed on requested/observed tab mismatch and include both IDs in receipts. Please prioritize this before any authenticated browser automation.

args.user_asks: “When I walk away, hide my authenticated browser tabs; when I return, restore them and tell me if anything changed.”
args.why_useful: The owner's browser sessions are the one place holding private logins, yet today they remain exposed whenever he steps away from the Mac. A worn pendant can provide a physical-presence signal that a browser extension alone cannot infer reliably. On departure, Safari would blur or lock configured sensitive tabs without closing sessions; on return, it would restore the view and deliver a compact change summary through the pendant. This combines the worn device, browser session, Mac enforcement, and relay in a way no single node can do.
args.model_tier: Use firmware/Mac deterministic presence and tab-lock logic; use a cheap background model only to summarize permitted page metadata after return. Realtime is unnecessary except when the owner asks a follow-up aloud.
args.latency_budget: Lock within 1–2 seconds of confirmed departure; restore within 2 seconds of return; summarize changes asynchronously and alert only when meaningful.
args.cost_estimate: Near-zero inference cost for presence and locking; occasional small summarization prompts dominate. Hardware cost is zero if a reliable existing pendant link can expose presence, otherwise a BLE-capable presence beacon is needed.
args.security_concerns: Fail closed on uncertain or lost presence, but never destroy sessions or submit actions. Keep page text out of durable storage; use existing short-lived browser findings and provenance. Ship an empty per-origin policy and require the owner to configure which origins may be locked, summarized, or spoken. The relay must not receive raw page contents merely because a tab changed.
missing: A signed, low-latency pendant-presence/absence signal exposed to the Mac agent
A Safari extension command to obscure and restore a tab without navigating or losing its authenticated session
A local encrypted snapshot of tab title/origin and a change-diff pipeline that can operate without storing page bodies
Owner-configurable per-origin lock and post-return summary policy

args.user_asks: “Put the confirmation I’m viewing into the right place on my phone.”
args.why_useful: The browser can reach the authenticated confirmation, but the iPhone is where the owner actually needs the resulting boarding pass, reservation, warranty, or appointment. The system should extract the structured artifact from Safari, create the native Calendar/Wallet/Files item through iPhone Mirroring, and report exactly what was created through the pendant. This removes the current manual bridge of screenshots, downloads, and retyping while preserving the authenticated session on the browser.
args.model_tier: Use deterministic typed extraction and native iOS actions wherever possible; use a small gpt-5.6-luna pass only to map page fields to an artifact schema. Realtime only speaks the completion summary.
args.latency_budget: 10–20 seconds for extraction and native app entry; if the page lacks a machine-readable artifact, produce a preview rather than guessing fields.
args.cost_estimate: One browser read plus a short structured extraction and several local iOS actions; inference cost is modest, with UI traversal dominating latency.
args.security_concerns: Never send credentials or page bodies to iOS. Show a preview of title/date/identifier before creating the artifact, preserve source URL and evidence, and make the created local item undoable. Keep page text ephemeral and honor the existing empty per-origin configuration until the owner defines it.
missing: A typed artifact schema and extractor for boarding passes, reservations, appointments, receipts, and warranty records
An iOS action that creates/imports those artifacts through the real native app rather than typing arbitrary page text
A reversible cross-surface receipt linking the created phone item to the browser evidence capsule
built_from: Existing ios_* actions through the Mac agent

args.user_asks: “I’ve lost control of my devices—lock every session now.”
args.why_useful: A physical pendant action is available even when the Mac screen, browser, or phone cannot be reached. One event should immediately lock the Mac, obscure authenticated Safari tabs, stop any pending browser command, and invoke the iPhone's lock/home path; the relay should record a short incident receipt and the pendant should confirm locally even if the network is down. This is a genuinely cross-node safety action, not something the browser or Mac can guarantee alone.
args.model_tier: No model is needed for the immediate lock fan-out. Use the realtime tier only to explain status afterward; background reconciliation can use a cheap model, if at all.
args.latency_budget: Local pendant acknowledgement under 500 ms; Mac/browser/iPhone fan-out within 2 seconds, with retries and an explicit list of surfaces that did or did not lock.
args.cost_estimate: Negligible inference cost; local serial/BLE or network fan-out dominates. Requires a durable incident receipt but no page content.
args.security_concerns: This is intentionally high-impact and must be a dedicated physical gesture that cannot be triggered by accidental audio. It should fail closed, preserve no page text, cancel queued browser mutations, and never claim a surface locked until its receipt confirms it. Recovery is owner-controlled re-authentication; do not silently delete sessions or data.
missing: A firmware panic gesture and local offline command path distinct from ordinary alert playback
A relay broadcast with delivery acknowledgements and idempotency
Mac/browser/iOS lock primitives with receipts and cancellation of queued actions
A pendant-visible status code for partial completion
built_from: Existing ios_* actions through the Mac agent

transcript.summary: Recorded two capabilities that are not in the backlog: turn an authenticated browser confirmation into a native iPhone artifact (Calendar/Wallet/Files) with provenance and undo, and a physical pendant panic action that locks Mac, Safari sessions, queued browser work, and iPhone with per-surface acknowledgements. The walk-away privacy-lock idea was rejected as an existing backlog item, so I did not restate it.
